(CNN) -- The Marine husband of a slain Fort Bragg soldier was charged with murder Monday and another Marine was charged with aiding the crime, a local police chief said. Fayetteville, North Carolina, police released this undated photo of 2nd Lt. Holley Wimunc. Authorities have been searching for the missing soldier, Army 2nd Lt. Holley Wimunc, 24, since a fire torched her North Carolina apartment on July 10. Marine Cpl. John Wimunc and fellow Marine Lance Cpl. Kyle Alden were initially charged with arson, but after police interviews Wimunc was charged with first-degree murder, said Fayetteville Police Chief Tom Bergamine. Alden was charged with felony accessory after the fact to first-degree murder, Bergamine said. Both were taken to Cumberland County's jail and held without bond, he said. Earlier, a witness found a charred body in woods, but Detective Jeff Locklear told reporters that police were still awaiting a positive identification from the medical examiner and could not say for certain it was Holley Wimunc. The lieutenant's father released a statement about the death Monday in which he said his daughter was a nurse at a military hospital and had two children. "It is with profound sadness that our family just received the news from authorities that our beloved daughter Holley is dead," Wimunc's father said in a statement released to CNN affiliate WRAL in Raleigh, North Carolina. "Since last Thursday's shocking news about Holley's burned apartment and her missing person status, our family through the country has nonetheless been holding on to a thin thread of hope that she would be found alive." Military officials said both Marines were stationed at Camp Lejeune, which is about two hours away from Wimunc's Fayetteville home. Joe Lenczyk -- resident agent-in-charge for the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives -- said Wimunc and her husband were estranged and lived apart. Wimunc is the second female soldier from Fort Bragg to die under suspicious circumstances in recent weeks. Spc. Megan Lynn Touma, 23, was seven months pregnant at the time of her death in June, authorities said. Investigators say they are treating that death as a homicide. Camp Lejeune also has had a suspicious death of a female soldier this year. Twenty-year-old pregnant Marine Lance Cpl. Maria Lauterbach's charred body was found January in the back yard of another Marine stationed at the base. That suspect, U.S. Marine Cpl. Cesar Laurean, was captured in April in Mexico.

(CNN) -- The Marine husband of a slain Fort Bragg soldier was charged with murder Monday, while a fellow Marine was charged with aiding in the crime, according to a local police chief.

Fayetteville, North Carolina, police released an undated photograph of 2nd Lt. Holley Wimunc. Authorities had been searching for the missing soldier, 24-year-old Army 2nd Lt. Holley Wimunc, since a fire engulfed her North Carolina apartment on July 10.

Marine Cpl. John Wimunc and fellow Marine Lance Cpl. Kyle Alden were initially charged with arson; however, following police interviews, Wimunc was subsequently charged with first-degree murder, said Fayetteville Police Chief Tom Bergamine. Alden was charged with being an accessory after the fact to first-degree murder, Bergamine added. Both men were taken to the Cumberland County jail and are being held without bond.

Earlier, a witness discovered a charred body in a wooded area, though Detective Jeff Locklear told reporters that police were still awaiting positive identification from the medical examiner and could not yet confirm whether the remains were those of Holley Wimunc.

The lieutenant's father released a statement on Monday confirming his daughter's death, describing her as a nurse at a military hospital and mother of two children. "It is with profound sadness that our family has just received the news from authorities that our beloved daughter Holley is dead," he said in a statement provided to CNN affiliate WRAL in Raleigh, North Carolina. "Since last Thursday's shocking news about Holley's burned apartment and her missing person status, our family and friends across the country have nonetheless held on to a thin thread of hope that she would be found alive."

Military officials confirmed that both Marines were stationed at Camp Lejeune, located roughly two hours from Wimunc's home in Fayetteville. Joe Lenczyk, resident agent-in-charge for the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, said that Wimunc and her husband were estranged and living separately at the time of her death.

Wimunc is the second female soldier from Fort Bragg to die under suspicious circumstances in recent weeks. Spc. Megan Lynn Touma, 23, was seven months pregnant at the time of her death in June, according to authorities, who are treating the case as a homicide.

Camp Lejeune has also experienced a suspicious death involving a female service member this year. The charred remains of 20-year-old pregnant Marine Lance Cpl. Maria Lauterbach were discovered in January in the backyard of a fellow Marine stationed at the base. The suspect in that case, U.S. Marine Cpl. Cesar Laurean, was apprehended in Mexico in April.

**Local Police Chief Announces Murder Charges in Fort Bragg Soldier Case**

According to a Fayetteville police chief, murder charges were filed Monday against the Marine husband of a Fort Bragg soldier who was killed, while a second Marine faces charges for helping conceal the crime.

The missing service member, 24-year-old Army 2nd Lt. Holley Wimunc, had not been seen since flames engulfed her North Carolina residence on July 10th, prompting an extensive search by authorities.

Police Chief Tom Bergamine reported that Marine Cpl. John Wimunc and his fellow service member, Lance Cpl. Kyle Alden, initially faced only arson charges. However, following additional questioning by investigators, prosecutors upgraded Wimunc's charge to first-degree murder. Alden, meanwhile, was booked on charges of being an accessory after the fact to that murder. Bergamine confirmed both men were transported to Cumberland County jail, where they remain without possibility of bail.

Prior to these charges, someone had discovered a burned body within a wooded area, though Detective Jeff Locklear cautioned reporters that confirmation from the medical examiner's office was still pending—meaning officials couldn't yet definitively link the remains to Wimunc.

In a statement issued Monday, the lieutenant's father confirmed his daughter's passing, describing her as a mother of two who worked as a nurse at a military medical facility.

"It is with profound sadness that our family just received the news from authorities that our beloved daughter Holley is dead," he wrote, in remarks shared with CNN's affiliate station WRAL based in Raleigh. He added that ever since news broke the previous Thursday about the apartment fire and her disappearance, relatives across the nation had clung to hope for her safe return, however slim that hope may have been.

Both Marines were assigned to Camp Lejeune, a base situated roughly two hours from where Wimunc lived in Fayetteville, according to military spokespersons.

Joe Lenczyk, who serves as resident agent-in-charge for the ATF, noted that the couple had been separated and were not living together at the time.

This marks the second instance in recent weeks of a female Fort Bragg soldier dying under circumstances that raised suspicion. Earlier, in June, 23-year-old Spc. Megan Lynn Touma died while seven months into her pregnancy—a case authorities are now investigating as a homicide.

Camp Lejeune itself experienced a similarly troubling incident earlier this year involving a female service member. In January, the burned remains of 20-year-old pregnant Marine Lance Cpl. Maria Lauterbach turned up in the backyard belonging to another Marine from that installation. The man accused in that case, Cpl. Cesar Laurean, was eventually apprehended in Mexico this past April.

*By Staff Correspondent*

When CNN's production team set out to profile Sergeant Michael Torres, they knew they had found a story that would resonate with viewers across the political spectrum. As a decorated Marine who had served three tours overseas, Torres represented the kind of narrative that combines personal sacrifice with broader questions about military service in America.

The segment, which aired during CNN's evening programming block, followed Torres through his daily routine at a veterans' support center in North Carolina. Cameras captured him mentoring younger service members, many of whom struggled with the transition back to civilian life after deployment. "The hardest part isn't the training or even combat," Torres told CNN correspondents during the interview. "It's coming home and figuring out who you are when the mission is over."

CNN's coverage highlighted not just Torres's individual story but the systemic challenges facing Marines and other veterans nationwide—issues ranging from mental health support to employment opportunities. The network's decision to feature his story reflected a broader journalistic commitment to humanizing military service beyond statistics and policy debates.

Viewers responded strongly to the piece, with many praising CNN for giving voice to perspectives often overlooked in mainstream news coverage. The segment sparked conversations on social media about veteran support systems and the personal costs of military service.

For Torres, the experience of being profiled by a major network like CNN offered an opportunity to advocate for fellow Marines. "If sharing my story helps even one veteran feel less alone," he said, "then it was worth stepping in front of that camera."

The piece stands as an example of how major news organizations continue to find compelling human interest stories within military communities, bridging the gap between those who serve and the civilian audiences who watch from home.
